note: Values are expressed in each system's base unit (Nephite: senum/senine; Israel: shekel; New Testament: denarius). Weights and exchange rates follow the text; modern-weight estimates are scholarly approximations.

systems.name: Nephite Money & Measures
systems.place: Zarahemla — the reign of the judges
systems.intro: When the lawyer Zeezrom tried to bribe Amulek, Mormon paused to lay out the whole Nephite system of gold and silver pieces and grain measures, reckoned 'according to their value.' It is the only place in scripture that spells out an entire monetary system unit by unit.
systems.anchor: 1 senine of gold  =  1 senum of silver  =  a measure of barley  =  a judge's wage for one day

items.name: Senine
items.note: The base gold piece — a judge received one for each day he sat.

items.name: Seon
items.note: Twice the value of a senine.

items.name: Shum
items.note: Twice a seon — four senines.

items.name: Limnah
items.note: 'The value of them all' — senine, seon and shum together.

items.name: Senum
items.note: Equal to a senine of gold, and to a measure of barley.

items.name: Amnor
items.note: As great as two senums.

items.name: Ezrom
items.note: As great as four senums.

items.name: Onti
items.note: 'As great as them all' — the greatest silver measure.

items.name: Shiblon
items.note: Half of a senum.

items.name: Shiblum
items.note: Half of a shiblon.

items.name: Leah
items.note: Half of a shiblum — the smallest measure.

items.name: Antion of gold
items.note: Equal to three shiblons — used in reckoning grain.

facts.d: A judge earned one senine of gold (or a senum of silver) for every day he sat in judgment — so corrupt judges stirred up contention to be paid for more days.
Zeezrom offered Amulek six onties of silver — forty-two days' wages — to deny the existence of a Supreme Being. Amulek refused.
A senine or senum bought a measure of barley, or of any grain — anchoring the whole system to daily bread.

systems.name: Weights of Ancient Israel
systems.intro: Before coins, silver was weighed out on a balance. Abraham 'weighed to Ephron four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant' for the cave of Machpelah. The shekel — literally 'a weight' — was the standard.
systems.anchor: 1 shekel of silver  =  20 gerahs  (the standard weight of silver)

items.name: Gerah
items.note: The smallest weight — one-twentieth of a shekel.

items.name: Bekah
items.note: Half a shekel — the 'ransom' every man paid for the sanctuary.

items.name: Pim
items.note: Two-thirds of a shekel — the Philistines' charge to sharpen a tool.

items.name: Shekel
items.note: The standard weight of silver (about 11 grams).

items.name: Mina (maneh)
items.note: Fifty shekels.

items.name: Talent
items.note: The largest weight — 3,000 shekels, roughly 34 kilograms.

facts.d: Joseph's brothers sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces — shekels — of silver.
Abraham paid 400 shekels of silver for the field and cave of Machpelah, the first foothold of the promised land.
Zechariah's 'goodly price' — thirty shekels, the value of a slave — became the wage of betrayal.

systems.name: Coins of the New Testament
systems.intro: By the Savior's day minted coins circulated — Roman denarii, Greek drachmas, and small Jewish copper. A denarius was a labourer's wage for a day; the smallest was the widow's mite, worth a fraction of a penny.
systems.anchor: 1 denarius (a 'penny')  =  a labourer's wage for one day

items.name: Lepton (mite)
items.note: The 'widow's mite' — the least coin of all; she cast in two.

items.name: Quadrans (farthing)
items.note: Two mites — the 'uttermost farthing.'

items.name: Assarion (farthing)
items.note: Two sparrows were sold for one of these.

items.name: Denarius (penny)
items.note: A day's wage, and the tribute coin — 'Render unto Caesar.'

items.name: Drachma
items.note: The Greek near-twin of the denarius — the coin the woman lost and swept to find.

items.name: Stater
items.note: Four drachmas — the coin Peter drew from the fish's mouth, paying the temple tax for two.

items.name: Thirty pieces of silver
items.note: Tyrian shekels (staters) — the price of betraying the Lord.

items.name: Mina (pound)
items.note: A hundred denarii — the 'pound' each servant was given to trade.

items.name: Talent
items.note: Six thousand denarii — the unmerciful servant owed ten thousand of them.

facts.d: A poor widow cast in two mites — 'all her living' — and the Lord said she had given more than all the rich.
Shown a denarius stamped with Caesar's image, Jesus said, 'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.'
The householder agreed with the labourers for a penny — a denarius — a day, then paid the last the same as the first.
